transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-30 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sarah Kim (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Laura Chen (Cosmos CTO), Miguel Alvarez (Platform Eng), Priya Singh (Head of ML)
Recording: (auto)

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
- Cosmos is evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted + private workloads; they care about integration with LangChain/LlamaIndex, proxy/gateway architecture, and strong observability.
- Main concerns: data residency for PII, KMS integration, per-route quotas and rate limiting, and end-to-end tracing for cost attribution.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Sarah Kim: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Sarah Kim from Redwood, and with me is Daniel Park our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Laura Chen: Good thanks Sarah. Appreciate you fitting us in. Quick note, we're in PST.
[00:12] Miguel Alvarez: Hey all, Miguel here. We'll be the one integrating into our platform.
[00:15] Priya Singh: Priya here, ML lead — mostly interested in runtime behaviour, caching, and quality regression checks.
[00:22] Sarah Kim: Awesome. Goal today is to understand your integration surface — SDK preferences, any agent/LLM orchestration stacks you use like LangChain or LlamaIndex, whether you're leaning Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, and what observability hooks you need. Daniel will jump in on technical details.
[00:33] Daniel Park: Hi — quick agenda: 1) current stack and OSS libs, 2) traffic and SLOs, 3) security/compliance, 4) SDK + integration patterns, 5) next steps.
[00:40] Laura Chen: Sounds good. High level: Cosmos runs a customer support assistant and product search augmentation. Production traffic today is small but we expect to ramp to 200–500 QPS in six months if tests pass. We run services on AWS EKS, VPC-enabled, all sensitive data must stay in our VPC or be encrypted with our KMS.
[00:58] Daniel Park: Ok that's helpful. On the VPC/KMS note — Redwood Private supports a customer-managed control plane or an on-prem option; Dedicated can be VPC peered and we can enable customer KMS integration.
[01:12] Miguel Alvarez: When you say peered, do you mean a VPN or direct connect type setup? We prefer direct connect but VPN is acceptable for pilot.
[01:20] Sarah Kim: Both are options — for initial POC we usually do secure VPN tunnels, then we can go Direct Connect/PrivateLink for Dedicated/Private later. We'll share a network diagram in the security pack.
[01:30] Priya Singh: From the ML side, we use LangChain for orchestration and LlamaIndex for retrieval-augmented features. We're mostly Python, but some Node microservices talk to the assistant as well.
[01:40] Daniel Park: Great — we have SDKs for Python and Node, plus an examples repo that shows LangChain integrations and LlamaIndex index loaders. We also provide a small adapter for the typical chain/agent pattern.
[01:52] Laura Chen: Can you walk through the typical integration pattern — e.g., do we point LangChain to Redwood as an endpoint, or is there a middleware/gateway you recommend?
[01:59] Daniel Park: Common patterns: 1) Direct SDK calls from backend service to Redwood Hosted API with per-service API keys; 2) A simple gateway/proxy in your VPC that routes requests to Redwood and handles auth, retries, and rate limits; 3) For private deployments you can run Redwood API gateway inside your network so calls never leave your VPC.
[02:16] Miguel Alvarez: For pattern 2, do you have a recommended gateway implementation? We run Envoy + Istio in EKS.
[02:23] Daniel Park: Envoy is a common choice. We publish an example envoy filter that injects the API key and does token based auth. With Istio you can also configure mTLS. We'll send the repo link.
[02:33] Priya Singh: How does rate limiting/quotas work? We need per-route quotas; e.g., customer support has different budgets than search.
[02:39] Sarah Kim: Redwood supports per-route quotas and rate limits on Hosted. For Dedicated/Private you can enforce quotas in your gateway or in Redwood's Dedicated control plane; we expose per-API-key and per-route configs. The Console also shows usage per-token and per-route so you can tie costs back to teams.
[02:53] Miguel Alvarez: If we put the gateway in front, is there any loss of streaming behavior or latency? Streaming is important for the assistant.
[02:59] Daniel Park: Not necessarily — we pass through streaming responses — our gateway example supports HTTP chunked transfer and server-sent events. Latency added by a proxy is usually a few ms; the bigger factors are batching and KV cache hits.
[03:12] Priya Singh: You mentioned KV cache — can you clarify how prefix caching and KV cache behave with LangChain-style RAG?
[03:18] Daniel Park: Sure. KV cache stores model key-value activations across requests to accelerate generation for repeated prefixes — it's especially helpful for chat-like workloads. For RAG via LlamaIndex, prefix caching helps if you have many repeated system prompts or assistant priming. For retrieval caching, we recommend caching embeddings/nearest-neighbor results (Pinecone, Weaviate) upstream; Redwood's prefix/KV cache is focused on autocompletions and autoregressive context speedups.
[03:40] Laura Chen: What's the overhead of enabling prefix cache? Any correctness issues?
[03:43] Daniel Park: It's transparent — we do cache invalidation based on context. For strict determinism you can turn off caching. In our experience it reduces token costs 10–40% depending on prompt reuse.
[03:53] Miguel Alvarez: If a customer uses LangChain with chains that call multiple models per request, do you recommend multiplexing via the gateway or letting services call Redwood directly?
[04:03] Daniel Park: For observability and quotas we often recommend centralizing through a gateway — you get consistent auth, per-route quotas, centralized retry/backoff logic, and unified request tracing. But for very low-latency critical paths, direct SDK calls are ok if you can manage keys and quotas.
[04:15] Priya Singh: Observability hooks — we need tracing per request and token-level cost attribution. How does Redwood expose those?
[04:21] Sarah Kim: Console has token-level cost breakdowns, and we expose tracing headers to correlate requests with your distributed traces. We also provide export hooks to Datadog, Honeycomb, and logs to your S3 or our hosted logs depending on deployment. For Private you can route logs to your ELK/Kinesis.
[04:36] Miguel Alvarez: Are there server-side webhooks for generation completion or only streaming?
[04:40] Daniel Park: Streaming is primary, but you can also enable a completion webhook for async workflows — we support callback URLs with HMAC verification.
[04:48] Laura Chen: On the security front, SOC2 is a must; can you support SAML SSO and RBAC?
[04:53] Sarah Kim: Yes — SSO via SAML/OIDC, role-based access controls, and audit logs are available for Dedicated and Private. Hosted customers get basic access controls and audit logs; Enterprise plan (Dedicated/Private) gets more retention and integrations.
[05:06] Priya Singh: For PII we want to encrypt data at rest with our KMS and ensure logs either never contain prompts or are redacted.
[05:13] Daniel Park: We support customer-managed KMS in Dedicated and Private. For Hosted we can integrate with your KMS via a customer-managed key in some cases or keep logs redacted as part of our compliance package — we'll share the dataflow diagram.
[05:25] Laura Chen: Regarding model variants and fallback — if your primary model is out of capacity can we auto-fall back to a cheaper model? We need predictable degradation.
[05:33] Daniel Park: Yes — we have routing policies. You can set a primary model and fallback variants (smaller quantized models) with policies by latency, cost, or region. If latency SLO is strict, you can route to Dedicated or to a lower-latency variant.
[05:46] Miguel Alvarez: Let's talk numbers: what's the expected latency for a 512-token generation on typical GPU-backed Dedicated vs Hosted?
[05:53] Daniel Park: It depends on model and seq length, but for a 13B model on our optimized Dedicated capacity you might see 150–300ms per token depending on batching; Hosted has slightly higher tail latency due to multi-tenant scheduling, typically p95 is 30–60ms higher. We can run a benchmark with your prompt set to get exact numbers.
[06:09] Priya Singh: How does batching interact with latency — are we likely to see high latency spikes if we enable batching?
[06:14] Daniel Park: There's a tradeoff. Batching increases throughput and reduces cost per token but adds scheduling latency. Redwood Optimize provides suggestions for tradeoffs and you can set per-route latency SLOs to bias towards lower latency (smaller batches) or lower cost (bigger batches).
[06:27] Laura Chen: On the SDK side, do you have ready-made LangChain LLM wrappers? We want to drop-in replace the OpenAI wrapper.
[06:34] Daniel Park: Yes — our SDK includes a LangChain-compatible LLM class and examples for LlamaIndex connectors. The repo has Python/Node examples showing prompt templates, streaming, and tool-calling patterns.
[06:44] Miguel Alvarez: Do you support function/tool calling (structured outputs)?
[06:47] Daniel Park: We do — structured output support and function calling is available; our client SDKs parse responses and we provide typed schemas for common patterns.
[06:54] Priya Singh: Any pitfalls when migrating from OpenAI endpoints to Redwood? We need to avoid prompt regressions.
[07:00] Sarah Kim: Main areas: prompt tokens differences between models, streaming semantics, and temperature/pen tuning. We recommend running an eval set (we can help onboard your prompt set into Redwood Evals to detect regressions).
[07:12] Miguel Alvarez: How do you handle quotas when multiple teams share a single API key? We might prefer per-service keys.
[07:18] Daniel Park: Per-service API keys are best practice — Redwood supports API keys per-project/team and per-route rules. You can also set per-key quotas in the Console.
[07:28] Laura Chen: We heard about observability with token-level cost. Can the console break down cost by prompt template?
[07:33] Sarah Kim: Yes — with route tags and request metadata (you can pass a route name or team id in headers) the Console groups usage by route/template, and you can export that to your billing system.
[07:44] Priya Singh: For our retrieval augmentation, we plan to use external vector DB — would Redwood host embeddings or do that upstream?
[07:51] Daniel Park: You can do either. Many customers compute embeddings and host them in Pinecone/Weaviate. Redwood can also provide embeddings endpoints and ephemeral caching to reduce calls, but for production RAG we typically recommend a dedicated vector DB.
[08:03] Miguel Alvarez: Is the embeddings format standard? We currently use cosine similarity and store 1536-d vectors.
[08:08] Daniel Park: Yes standard floats, and our SDKs interoperate with common vector stores. We'll include connectors examples.
[08:15] Laura Chen: On billing and cost predictability — we want to cap spend per team each month. Does Redwood support hard spend caps?
[08:22] Sarah Kim: We support quotas that effectively cap token usage per API key; for Hosted we can enforce hard caps per key and send alerts. For Dedicated, you're on committed capacity so it's a different model — we'd work with you on commit sizing.
[08:36] Priya Singh: For our pilot we want Hosted + gateway in our VPC so logs and traces are sent to our observability stack — is that possible?
[08:44] Daniel Park: Yes — you can run a lightweight gateway in your VPC that forwards to Hosted. That gateway can enrich traces and forward logs to your stack; we provide trace headers and examples for Datadog/Honeycomb.
[08:56] Laura Chen: Performance testing — what's the usual approach? We want to run a smoke test and then a sustained run to emulate 200–500 QPS.
[09:04] Daniel Park: Typical flow: 1) small smoke test with your sample prompts (<1k requests), 2) a benchmark run with ramping load and the same prompt distribution, 3) regression test for output quality with your eval set. We can run the benchmarking from our side or provide a test harness.
[09:16] Miguel Alvarez: For the benchmarking, can you record per-request traces and correlate them with token costs? We need to map slow requests to token billing anomalies.
[09:23] Daniel Park: Yes — traces include token counts and cost estimates; we can export detailed logs for benchmark runs.
[09:30] Priya Singh: If we do a Private deployment on-prem, how long does setup usually take? We have hardware and networking teams ready.
[09:36] Sarah Kim: On-prem/private timeline varies — small POC can be done in weeks if you provide infra and network access; full production on-prem can take 6–12 weeks depending on compliance and change windows. Dedicated in our cloud is faster — usually 2–4 weeks for reserved capacity.
[09:50] Laura Chen: Any constraints on supported GPUs or runtimes? We run a mix of Ampere A100 and newer Hopper in our infra.
[09:57] Daniel Park: We support common GPU families, and our runtime optimizes kernels per architecture. For on-prem we’ll confirm driver/python and container runtime versions.
[10:05] Sarah Kim: Quick recap — Cosmos needs: LangChain/LlamaIndex SDK examples, gateway pattern for Envoy/Istio, per-route quotas and spend caps, tracing integration with Datadog, KMS integration for secrets, and a benchmark run for 200–500 QPS. Next steps are in a ticket Sarah will follow up on.
[10:22] Laura Chen: Sounds good. A couple of quick clarifying Qs — do you have a limit on number of API keys or projects?
[10:27] Daniel Park: No hard limit — most customers create many keys per environment/team. We do recommend organizing them per-service.
[10:33] Miguel Alvarez: One more — about fallback routing: can we set region-based fallbacks to keep traffic in EU for some customers?
[10:39] Daniel Park: Yes — routing policies support region affinity and fallbacks. We also support model pinning per-route.
[10:46] Priya Singh: For the LangChain wrapper, is streaming integrated into the LLM class or do we need a separate approach?
[10:51] Daniel Park: Streaming is integrated — the LangChain wrapper supports event-stream listeners and incremental callbacks.
[10:58] Laura Chen: Any known gotchas around tooling like LlamaIndex? We run into tokenization differences sometimes.
[11:03] Daniel Park: Tokenization differences and prompt formatting are the common gotchas; we recommend normalizing tokenization in preprocessing and keeping a small eval suite.
[11:12] Sarah Kim: Ok — let's align on deliverables. Daniel will put together SDK snippets + LangChain/LlamaIndex examples. I'll send pricing + security pack and we'll sync on a date for the Private deep dive.
[11:23] Laura Chen: Great, thanks. We can target the deep dive week of 2026-05-11.
[11:28] Sarah Kim: Perfect. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the notes and links.
[11:33] (meeting ends)
